topIssues.title: kona/derive: derivation pipeline invariant analysis — bad L1 input must never halt derivation
topIssues.author: sebastianst
topIssues.body:
## Summary

Invariant analysis of the kona derivation pipeline at `rust/kona/crates/protocol/derive/`, mirroring the Go op-node analysis in #19491.

**Invariant**: No malformed or bad external input (batcher transactions, system config logs, deposit transactions from L1) should cause derivation to stop. Bad input should be dropped and processing should continue. Only logic errors are allowed to cause pipeline-halting (Critical) errors.

## Findings

All pipeline stages are correctly implemented **except for two issues**:

| Stage | File | Status |
|-------|------|--------|
| Traversal | `stages/traversal/` | ✅ System config errors ignored with warn |
| L1 Retrieval | `stages/l1_retrieval.rs` | ✅ |
| Frame Queue | `stages/frame_queue.rs` | ✅ Malformed frames silently dropped |
| Channel Bank | `stages/channel/channel_bank.rs` | ✅ |
| Channel Assembler | `stages/channel/channel_assembler.rs` | ✅ |
| Channel Reader | `stages/channel/channel_reader.rs` | ✅ |
| Batch Queue (pre-Holocene) | [`stages/batch/batch_queue.rs:388-390`](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/blob/48b31f0b1b1e9afcf4d07f75c28771f602cc6a1b/rust/kona/crates/protocol/derive/src/stages/batch/batch_queue.rs#L388-L390) | ⚠️ See 19511 |
| Batch Stream (post-Holocene) | `stages/batch/batch_stream.rs` | ✅ |
| Attributes Builder | [`attributes/stateful.rs:114-120`](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/blob/48b31f0b1b1e9afcf4d07f75c28771f602cc6a1b/rust/kona/crates/protocol/derive/src/attributes/stateful.rs#L114-L120) | ⚠️ See 19512 |
| Calldata Source | `sources/calldata.rs` | ✅ |
| Blob Source | `sources/blobs.rs` | ✅ |

## Sub-issues

- 19511 — `batch_queue.rs`: span batch extraction failure returns `Critical` instead of flushing and continuing
- 19512 — `stateful.rs`: system config update errors return `Critical` instead of being ignored

## Notes

- Deposit errors in `stateful.rs` returning `Critical` are **intentional** — matches Go op-node behaviour (deposits may never be silently dropped)
- `BatchValidity::Past` returning `Critical` pre-Holocene is **intentional** — should never be reached with valid external data

## Related

Companion to Go op-node analysis: #19491

---

topIssues.title: checkSpanBatch does not enforce activation-block user-tx rule that checkSingularBatch enforces
topIssues.author: trasnake87
topIssues.body:
`op-node/rollup/derive/batches.go` enforces the activation-block "no user transactions" rule (per spec [optimism/specs#791](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/specs/pull/791) and issue #17704) for singular batches but not for span batches. The same activation block, encoded as a span batch, is accepted.

### Where

`checkSingularBatch` (batches.go around L137) drops the batch:

```go
if (cfg.IsJovianActivationBlock(batch.Timestamp) ||
    cfg.IsKarstActivationBlock(batch.Timestamp) ||
    cfg.IsInteropActivationBlock(batch.Timestamp)) &&
    len(batch.Transactions) > 0 {
    log.Warn("dropping batch with user transactions in fork activation block")
    return BatchDrop
}
```

`checkSpanBatch` (batches.go L308–L445) validates timestamps, sequencer drift, deposit/SetCode tx exclusion per block, but never checks `IsJovianActivationBlock` / `IsKarstActivationBlock` / `IsInteropActivationBlock` against `batch.GetBlockTransactions(i)`.

History: PR #14797 added the rule for Isthmus (singular only, closed), PR #17984 added it for Jovian (singular only, merged), PR #19250 added Karst to the same condition (singular only, merged). PR #19150 separately added the SetCode check to span (`fix(op-node): add SetCodeTxType check to span batch validation`) — same kind of singular/span asymmetry, fixed in isolation. The activation-block rule appears to have been missed across all three iterations.

### Reproduction

A short unit test against `CheckBatch` builds the same activation-block user transaction twice — singular returns `BatchDrop`, span returns `BatchAccept`:

```go
package derive

import (
    "context"
    "math/big"
    "math/rand"
    "testing"

    "github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/op-core/forks"
    "github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/op-node/rollup"
    "github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/op-service/eth"
    "github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/op-service/testutils"
    "github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum/common/hexutil"
    "github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum/core/types"
    "github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum/log"
    "github.com/stretchr/testify/require"
)

func TestSpanBatchActivationBlockUserTx(t *testing.T) {
    rng := rand.New(rand.NewSource(0x51a75))
    chainID := big.NewInt(10)
    signer := types.NewLondonSigner(chainID)
    tx := testutils.RandomTx(rng, big.NewInt(1_000_000_000), signer)
    txData, err := tx.MarshalBinary()
    require.NoError(t, err)

    for _, fork := range []forks.Name{forks.Jovian, forks.Karst, forks.Interop} {
        t.Run(string(fork), func(t *testing.T) {
            l1A := eth.L1BlockRef{Hash: testutils.RandomHash(rng), Number: 100, Time: 1_000}
            l2Safe := eth.L2BlockRef{
                Hash: testutils.RandomHash(rng), Number: 200, Time: l1A.Time,
                L1Origin: l1A.ID(), ParentHash: testutils.RandomHash(rng),
            }
            cfg := &rollup.Config{
                Genesis:           rollup.Genesis{L2Time: l2Safe.Time},
                BlockTime:         2,
                SeqWindowSize:     4,
                MaxSequencerDrift: 30,
            }
            activationTime := l2Safe.Time + cfg.BlockTime
            cfg.ActivateAt(fork, activationTime)

            singular := &SingularBatch{
                ParentHash: l2Safe.Hash, EpochNum: rollup.Epoch(l1A.Number),
                EpochHash: l1A.Hash, Timestamp: activationTime,
                Transactions: []hexutil.Bytes{txData},
            }
            singularValidity := CheckBatch(context.Background(), cfg, log.New(),
                []eth.L1BlockRef{l1A}, l2Safe,
                &BatchWithL1InclusionBlock{L1InclusionBlock: l1A, Batch: singular}, nil)
            require.Equal(t, BatchValidity(BatchDrop), singularValidity)

            span := initializedSpanBatch([]*SingularBatch{{
                ParentHash: l2Safe.Hash, EpochNum: rollup.Epoch(l1A.Number),
                EpochHash: l1A.Hash, Timestamp: activationTime,
                Transactions: []hexutil.Bytes{txData},
            }}, cfg.Genesis.L2Time, chainID)

            spanValidity := CheckBatch(context.Background(), cfg, log.New(),
                []eth.L1BlockRef{l1A}, l2Safe,
                &BatchWithL1InclusionBlock{L1InclusionBlock: l1A, Batch: span}, nil)
            require.Equal(t, BatchValidity(BatchAccept), spanValidity,
                "span batches bypass activation-block user tx filtering")
        })
    }
}
```

`go test ./op-node/rollup/derive -run TestSpanBatchActivationBlockUserTx -v` passes for jovian, karst, and interop on `develop` (verified at `be742e31a`).

### Suggested fix

Apply the same condition inside `checkSpanBatch`'s per-block loop, before the per-tx validation:

```go
if (cfg.IsJovianActivationBlock(blockTimestamp) ||
    cfg.IsKarstActivationBlock(blockTimestamp) ||
    cfg.IsInteropActivationBlock(blockTimestamp)) &&
    len(batch.GetBlockTransactions(i)) > 0 {
    log.Warn("dropping span batch with user transactions in fork activation block")
    return BatchDrop
}
```

For symmetry with `checkSingularBatch` and consistency with the spec rule.

### Notes

The action test `TestActivationBlockTxOmission` added in #17984 uses `helpers.NewBatcherCfg()` which produces span batches by default (Delta+ fork, `ForceSubmitSingularBatch=false` → `useSpanChannelOut=true`). I have not run that test against current `develop`; if it currently passes, there is an additional path catching this that I have missed.

topIssues.title: kona-sp1: Avoid repeating L1 derivation for every super-range transition
topIssues.author: Inphi
topIssues.body:
## Summary

The super-range guest currently creates a fresh derivation pipeline for every progressing `(timestamp, chain)` transition. Consecutive transitions therefore repeat overlapping L1 and DA work, including pipeline reset, L1 traversal, channel reconstruction, and batch decoding.

This may be a major contributor to proving latency. As one production data point, proving only 12 seconds of superchain time on SPN took over 30 minutes, without an obvious indication that the prover was resource-constrained.

## Current behavior

`build_range_outputs` calls `run_super_range_transition` independently for every claimed transition:

```rust
for transition in &inputs.claimed_transitions {
    let boot_info = run_super_range_transition(...).await?;
    validate_range_transition_output(...).await?;
}
```

Each progressing transition creates new L1/L2 providers, a new cursor, and a new derivation pipeline. Provider caches are discarded, the pipeline walks backward to reconstruct its starting state, and derivation scans forward through an L1/DA window that substantially overlaps adjacent transitions.

Relevant code:

- `rust/kona/sp1/crates/ethereum/client/src/super_range.rs`
- `rust/kona/crates/proof/proof/src/sync.rs`
- `rust/kona/crates/proof/proof/src/l1/pipeline.rs`
- `rust/kona/crates/protocol/derive/src/pipeline/core.rs`

This duplication also occurs when multiple timestamps are already included in one proposer chunk.

## Preliminary benchmark

A local single-chain devnet benchmark compared the current implementation with one continuous pipeline deriving the same blocks from the same agreed root and L1 head. The continuous run reproduced the exact final output root.

| Range | Current | Continuous | Cycle reduction | Guest wall reduction |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 2 L2 blocks | 561.4M cycles, 5.51s | 303.4M cycles, 4.58s | 46.0% | 17.0% |
| 3 L2 blocks | 970.5M cycles, 8.52s | 365.6M cycles, 4.86s | 62.3% | 42.9% |

For the three-block run, payload derivation fell from 939.2M to 344.7M cycles. It accounted for 98.3% of the total savings. Block execution was nearly unchanged at 3.68M versus 3.59M cycles.

Merging separate chunks without reusing the pipeline saved only approximately 5–6% of guest cycles. Increasing chunk size alone therefore does not address the repeated derivation.

### Important limitation

These devnet blocks had very little L2 activity. Block execution represented only about 0.4% of guest cycles, so the benchmark likely overstates the percentage reduction expected on a busy production chain.

On OP Mainnet near the 30M L2 gas limit, EVM execution may become a much larger share of total cycles. Conversely, derivation may also become more expensive because it must process larger compressed batches, more transaction data, and potentially more DA inputs. L2 gas is not a direct proxy for zkVM cycles, so this needs to be measured using real chain data.

The devnet result establishes that repeated derivation exists and is expensive for low-activity blocks. It does not yet establish the proportional end-to-end benefit on OP Mainnet or explain the full 30-minute SPN result.

## Proposed direction

Maintain one monotonically advancing derivation session per chain within a super-range proof:

1. Initialize the providers, cursor, pipeline, and executor from the earliest agreed output.
2. Traverse L1 and DA inputs once as timestamps advance.
3. Execute each newly required L2 block.
4. Validate every intermediate claimed output root and block hash.
5. Validate no-op timestamps without restarting derivation.
6. Preserve the existing timestamp-major public output ordering.

Pipeline reuse should initially remain inside one guest execution. Reusing state between independent child proofs would require a cryptographically bound derivation-state commitment.

## OP Mainnet follow-up

Before estimating production impact, repeat the comparison on several finalized OP Mainnet intervals, including a 12-second interval with blocks close to the 30M gas limit.

Measure for both the current and continuous paths:

- Total and per-phase guest cycles.
- Guest execution wall time.
- Witness size and collection time.
- L2 gas, transaction count, and compressed DA size.
- Exact final output-root equality.
- If practical, actual SPN proving time and queue/proving breakdown.

The Mainnet test requires a historical L1 execution RPC, an L1 Beacon endpoint with the required blob sidecars, and a proof-capable OP Mainnet L2 endpoint supporting historical `debug_executePayload`, raw headers/receipts, and `eth_getProof`.

## Acceptance criteria

- At most one derivation pipeline initialization per chain within a super-range proof.
- Existing range and aggregation public-output bindings remain unchanged.
- Tests cover multiple progressing transitions, intervening no-op timestamps, and multiple chains.
- A benchmark demonstrates at least a 10% guest-cycle improvement when multiple transitions progress.
- OP Mainnet measurements are recorded before making production-latency claims.

topPRs.title: interop: suspend atomic demo router execution
topPRs.author: opsuperchain
topPRs.body:
Stacked on #22840. The atomic demo now supports nested cross-chain callbacks while retaining one live OP EVM transaction per chain. A on chain A calls B on chain B; B uses the same facade/router mechanism to call a distinct C on chain A; C sees A's pending state and can call back into the still-running B. The callback executes inside each chain's original transaction, preserving pending storage, transient storage, origin, gas ancestry and rollback. Each included chain receives one final replay after callback/result tapes and access lists are materialized; divergence rejects the candidate without discovery restarts or padding.

Canonical callback dispatch runs through ordinary router bytecode. Gas remains local to each chain: top-level application calls have fixed budgets, while callbacks receive half the remaining gas at their dispatch point. Caller context is restored on return, scheduling depth is capped at 32, and the bundle-wide call limit still applies. Failed callback hints force application rollback even if caught. ERC-4337 uses the existing EntryPoint and demo paymaster for normal on-chain gas settlement; it does not reimburse off-chain discovery or prove that a builder honestly attempted success. Existing Go and Kona cycle algorithms remain unchanged.

The Go/devstack bridge uses pinned candidate-prefix state and exact signed envelopes. This is a **demo node integration**; production payload-service admission/publication and a single-signature wallet flow remain out of scope. ETH forwarding, STATICCALL facades and committing after a caught remote failure remain unsupported. The original Go discovery path remains available for root-driven calls; nested dispatch is connected to the suspended builder.

Validation passed: all 18 contracts PR checks; full developer contract suite (2,290 passed, 183 skipped) and optimized suite (2,350 passed, 159 skipped); all 40 Rust builder tests with artifact-dependent tests enabled, including optimized bytecode; full Rust workspace lint/rustdoc and Go lint; Go bridge/message/filter/verifier tests; and Go/Kona nested-cycle regressions. All four real-node suspended/nested ERC-4337 success/revert cases pass, including exact receipt gas/log parity and sponsor settlement. Contract checks used the configured Foundry remappings plus explicit Solady/OpenZeppelin mappings with automatic remapping disabled to avoid the local duplicate `src/src` import issue.

Solidity, Rust lifecycle/application-effect and Go reviews are complete; all findings were fixed, none dismissed. Shared node fixtures are included by the normal contracts artifact build. #22840's branch remains unchanged.

CI on `ac7332b5d4af30420badf96e670243ec59df941d` is complete but not green: title/dependency checks and five Wiz scanners passed; Wiz SAST was skipped. The x86 multicannon package built, then [artifact attestation failed because the fork workflow lacks `id-token` permission](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/actions/runs/34524915489/job/103031802906), reproducing the previous head's permission failure. The other seven package jobs were canceled by fail-fast; image/smoke jobs were skipped. Full upstream CI for this fork still requires human authorization.

topPRs.title: interop: atomic demo
topPRs.author: opsuperchain
topPRs.body:
This atomic demo lets an application call a remote contract through its normal ABI, use the returned value in subsequent calls, and roll back when the remote call or its own final check fails. CREATE2 facades provide predictable local addresses. Serial discovery constructs transactions across N chains using the existing CrossL2Inbox, access-list requirements, and cycle rules; no existing protocol contract or execution-client rule changes.

The sponsored path uses signed ERC-4337 UserOperations, the preinstalled EntryPoint, CREATE2 smart accounts, and an opt-in paymaster. Both successful and reverting application calls consume sponsored gas without requiring ETH in the smart accounts. EntryPoint catches application reverts, so its outer receipt succeeds while the UserOperation event reports failure. The builder bounds discovery, performs one final canonical replay per included chain, checks results and message commitments, and returns the exact verified UserOperations and outer calldata/fee parameters.

Failed result hints force rollback but cannot prove that a user caused the failure. Account owners explicitly authorize sponsorship spending; there is no user billing for discarded simulations, deliberate gas burning, or public builder admission service. Discovery still restarts transactions and uses local signers for intermediate operations. Nested callbacks, ETH/view facades, interactive signed intents, SDM refund reconciliation, and a production adapter for the complete candidate block environment remain outside this prototype. In particular, the RPC adapter retains the parent's base fee and cannot guarantee gas-price-sensitive execution against a changed next-block environment. See `op-test-sequencer/atomic/DESIGN.md` for these boundaries.

Capability regression coverage and the demo are separate commits. Go and contract/security reviews cover the sponsored extension; the fee mismatch found during review is fixed with EVM/RPC regressions and pinned submission fees. A gas-trace regression also checks identical gas supplied and consumed at the application and both proxy calls between final discovery and replay, after fixing the discovery adapter's cold inbox-address surcharge. The original capability changes also received Rust and CI reviews. No review findings were dismissed.

Local validation passes for all 17 contract PR checks, the tagged EVM suite, affected Go verification packages, Go lint/module checks, and both sponsored real op-reth/supernode scenarios. The node tests verify application rollback, UserOperation success/failure, the exact paymaster deposit debit, and unfunded smart accounts. The full optimized contract suite passes with 2,335 tests and 159 skips; the final developer-mode suite passes with 2,275 tests and 183 skips. An earlier developer run was invalidated by concurrent artifact-cache replacement; the sequential rerun above is clean. The original raw node scenarios, ten native Kona cycle tests, and CI routing scenarios also passed.

Full Kona/challenger execution remains blocked at setup by missing prestate artifacts; workspace Rust clippy is blocked by missing m4 in an unrelated native dependency, and local CircleCI schema/process validation is unavailable because its CLI is absent. Native cycle tests do not substitute for full proof execution. Main upstream CI requires human authorization under the repository's fork policy.

On the current commit, GitHub dependency, title, and all Wiz checks pass. The image workflow fails at [APK provenance attestation](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/actions/runs/34422616906/job/102701496534) with `missing "id-token" permission`, the same restricted-fork failure seen on the prior head; the other image builds are canceled and downstream image/smoke jobs are skipped. This draft is not CI-green.

topPRs.title: feat: interop message-expiry refunds (censorship escape hatch for SuperchainETHBridge)
topPRs.author: opsuperchain
topPRs.body:
# feat: interop message-expiry refunds (censorship escape hatch for SuperchainETHBridge)

## Problem

Interop **executing messages cannot be force-included via deposit transactions** — `CrossL2Inbox.validateMessage` requires the message checksum slot to be warm via the tx's EIP-2930 access list, and deposits have no access list (upstream even added an explicit `CrossL2Inbox_NoExecutingDeposits` guard). So the force-inclusion path that normally defeats sequencer censorship does **not** work for interop: if a destination sequencer refuses to relay an executing message, delivery is impossible.

For `SuperchainETHBridge.sendETH` this strands funds: the ETH is burned into `ETHLiquidity` on the **source** before the message is sent, and only minted on the destination inside `relayETH`. A censored relay means the ETH is burned on A and never minted on B — permanently in flight, with no way for the sender to recover it. Interop ETH therefore lacks the "always recoverable to the sender" property that L1↔L2 bridging has.

## Key protocol fact this builds on

`MESSAGE_EXPIRY_WINDOW` (7 days, per-depset configurable) is a **protocol validity rule**, enforced both at cross-safety (op-supernode invalidates heads carrying expired executing messages) and **in the fault proof** (kona's `MessageGraph` forces a deposit-only replacement block). Once a destination chain's clock passes `initiatingTimestamp + window` with the message still unrelayed, **delivery is permanently impossible** — no valid block can ever relay it. This PR turns that permanent fact into a recoverable refund, riding only existing censorship-resistant rails (withdrawals and deposits). It does **not** add any new expiry machinery and does **not** modify `L2ToL2CrossDomainMessenger`.

## Mechanism

For a message `H` sent A→B that was never relayed on B:

1. **B (attest)** — anyone calls `MessageExpiryRelay.attestUndelivered(H, sourceChainId, minGas)`. The relay checks the local `L2ToL2CrossDomainMessenger.successfulMessages(H) == false` and exports `(H, sourceChainId, block.timestamp)` to the `MessageExpiryHub` on L1 via B's ordinary L2→L1 withdrawal. (This is *not* an executing message, so if B censors it, it is itself force-includable as a deposit.)
2. **L1 (route)** — after the withdrawal finalizes, `MessageExpiryHub.receiveExpiryNotice` authenticates the calling L1CrossDomainMessenger and its cluster, records the notice, then `forwardExpiryNotice` deposits it into the source chain via A's L1CrossDomainMessenger (force-includable).
3. **A (consume)** — `MessageExpiryRelay.receiveExpiry` verifies the attestation against the recorded send: the attestor must equal the recorded destination and `attestedAt` must be strictly beyond `recordedAt + expiryWindow`. It then notifies the sending application once.
4. **App (refund)** — `SuperchainETHBridge.onMessageExpired` re-mints the burned ETH and force-sends it back to the original sender.

**No double-spend:** the attestation only exists if `H` was undelivered; the refund only fires once `attestedAt > recordedAt + expiryWindow`; past the window, delivery is protocol-impossible; and both the relay record and the bridge's pending-send entry are deleted before any external call. Delivery and refund are mutually exclusive.

## Reusable primitive

The escape hatch is **not** ETH-bridge-specific. Any L2 contract that sends interop messages can opt in:
- call `MessageExpiryRelay.recordSentMessage(...)` when it sends (preimage-verified, so only the actual sender can register as the handler for a message hash), and
- implement `IMessageExpiryHandler.onMessageExpired(msgHash, attestorChainId, attestedAt)` to compensate.

`SuperchainETHBridge` is the first consumer and the reference integration.

## SuperchainETHBridge diff (minimal)

`1.0.1 → 1.1.0`. `sendETH` records the pending send and registers with the relay (guarded by a code-size check so non-interop chains are unaffected); new `onMessageExpired` refunds the sender. `relayETH` and everything else are untouched. The contract previously had zero storage; `pendingETHSends` is added at slot 0.

## New contracts

- `src/L2/MessageExpiryRelay.sol` — predeploy `0x42…2E` (proxied, interop-gated), both source-side (record/receive) and destination-side (attest) roles; same address on every chain.
- `src/L1/MessageExpiryHub.sol` — ownerless L1 singleton that routes notices between the chains of an interop cluster. Cluster membership is derived on-chain per call (SystemConfig ↔ L1CrossDomainMessenger ↔ OptimismPortal bidirectional binding + shared ETHLockbox authorization + shared AnchorStateRegistry); notices are namespaced by the cluster's lockbox so chains with colliding IDs across clusters cannot interfere.
- `interfaces/L2/IMessageExpiryHandler.sol` — the opt-in callback interface.

Predeploy wired through `Predeploys.sol`, `L2ContractsManager` (`→ 1.15.0`), `L2Genesis`, the Go predeploy registry, and the NUT upgrade bundle. The relay proxy ships **uninitialized** (fails closed); `hub`/`expiryWindow` are set post-deploy by the ProxyAdmin owner.

## Testing

- **Unit (forge):** full auth + boundary matrices for all three contracts, including sender-binding, exact expiry off-by-one, cross-cluster non-interference, and the refund end-state. (~70 tests.)
- **Acceptance (`op-acceptance-tests/tests/interop/expiry`, in-process two-chain interop devnet):** end-to-end — `sendETH` A→B, never relay, wait past a 12s expiry window, attest on B, prove + finalize the withdrawal on L1, forward through the hub, deposit into A, assert the sender is refunded exactly and all records are cleared. Plus a delivered-message regression guard (normal relay still works on the 1.1.0 bridge, and attesting a delivered message reverts). Runs without time-travel by shrinking the L1 dispute windows via new deployer options.

## Security

Two independent adversarial reviews were run. Both found the same **critical** in an earlier revision — the hub authenticated the incoming messenger but not the portal, letting a forged SystemConfig point at a real cluster-authorized portal and mint a false notice. **Fixed** by binding `portal.systemConfig() == systemConfig` (plus a registration-overwrite guard, notice-key namespacing by source chain, an attestation-timestamp bound, a monotone `expiryWindow` setter + `hub` setter for remediation, and a contract-handler requirement). Details and the list of attacks that were tried and failed are in the review notes.

## Known follow-ups (not in this PR)

- **Deploy/init wiring:** this is contracts-first. A production rollout needs a deploy script for `MessageExpiryHub` and an OPCM/governance step to `initialize` each relay proxy (`hub`, `expiryWindow`). The feature fails closed until then.
- **`expiryWindow` ↔ depset coupling:** the relay's window must be ≥ the dependency-set message-expiry window, but there is no on-chain link on L2 today (it is trusted ProxyAdmin-owner config, guarded only by the monotone setter). When the protocol exposes the depset window on-chain, self-validate.
- **Hub guardian pause:** considered as an incident kill-switch, deliberately omitted to avoid adding a trust role to an ownerless singleton; remediation today is re-pointing relays via `setHub`.
- Cluster liquidity/ASR migrations strand pending notices until re-attested (multi-day, recoverable).

topPRs.title: kona-sp1: build shared scenario world
topPRs.author: Inphi
topPRs.body:
## Summary

* Add a crate-private `ScenarioWorld` shared by fake L1, superroot, clock, proof, and action ports.
* Model immutable L1 snapshots, independent clocks and visibility, scripted failures, transaction lifecycles, barriers, and target-aware journals.
* Use the real prestate cache with zero retry delay and support prestate publication, initialization, and proposer restart.
* Add deterministic scenario coverage for confirmations, concurrent tasks, signer serialization, transaction uncertainty, failure boundaries, and restart behavior.

## Why

The existing fakes work well for focused tests, but they make longer proposer histories difficult to set up and reason about. This adds a shared world so effects from one cycle, such as a confirmed transaction, are visible to later reads, while tests retain precise control over timing, failures, and blocked tasks. This provides the foundation for the upcoming policy scenarios without adding production test hooks.

Part of #22171

topPRs.title: kona-sp1: add multi-cycle proposer policy scenarios
topPRs.author: Inphi
topPRs.body:
## Summary

Adds comprehensive multi-cycle proposer policy coverage using the deterministic `ScenarioWorld` and `ScenarioHarness`.

The scenarios cover:

- Frozen proposal horizons and long foreign-game histories
- Concurrent defense while creation is stalled
- Trusted and untrusted superroot contradictions
- Timed-out creation, late inclusion, and duplicate-creation guards
- Invalid topology, ownership, resolution, claim, and payout policy
- Independent pinned L1, latest L1, host, safe, and finalized clocks
- Factory, pending-game, and cached-game read-failure isolation
- Fresh proposer reconstruction over existing confirmed history

The scenario world now supports:

- L1 read faults keyed by boundary, target, and attempt
- Superroot query journaling with trust and L1 metadata
- Fresh proposer restarts over persistent world state
- Small history mutation controls required by the policy scenarios

The scenarios also exposed and fix a creation-safety issue:

- Game creation now requires a trusted superroot response before querying the UUID or submitting a bonded transaction.
- Trusted claim mismatches are terminal regardless of creator; untrusted observations remain retryable.
- The duplicate-creation guard is cleared when its tracked game becomes terminal or when factory history resets.

Treating a trusted contradiction as terminal may immediately release the creation guard and allow a
replacement at the same timestamp, putting a second bond at risk if the trusted response itself is
wrong. This is intentional: trusted supernode responses are the proposer's canonicality boundary;
retaining the guard would otherwise block recovery indefinitely at a frozen horizon.

Proof deadlines continue to use latest L1 chain time, matching the on-chain `block.timestamp` deadline check.

No launch, devstack, or acceptance-test configuration changes are required.
